summary.text: Student's t-test is a statistical test of whether the difference between the response of two groups is statistically significant.
It is any hypothesis test whose test statistic follows a Student's t-distribution under the null hypothesis, and it most commonly tests whether the means of two populations differ.
The distribution is named for William Sealy Gosset, who published it in 1908 under the pseudonym Student while working at the Guinness Brewery in Dublin.

items.prompt: Researchers enroll 100 people and randomly assign 50 to a treatment and 50 to a control group. Which form of the t-test fits?

options.label: Paired, because everyone is measured once
Paired, because the two groups have equal size
Neither, because it needs two measurements per person
Unpaired, because the groups are two separate sets of people

items.explain: With two non-overlapping, independent samples, the unpaired (independent samples) form of the t-test is used.

items.prompt: A clinic measures each patient's blood pressure before and after a drug, then compares each patient's own two numbers. Why is this design attractive?

options.label: It removes random differences between patients, raising power
It cuts the number of examinations the study needs
It makes the two groups independent of each other
It makes a null hypothesis unnecessary for the test

items.explain: Each patient serves as their own control, eliminating the random variation between patients. The price is that every subject must be examined twice.

items.prompt: A dataset keeps growing to a very large size. How do the results of a t-test and a Z-test compare?

options.label: They grow steadily more different from each other
They become very similar, as the t-test approaches the Z-test
The Z-test always reaches a decision before the t-test
The t-test can no longer be computed at that size

items.explain: In many cases a Z-test yields very similar results, because the t-test converges to the Z-test as the dataset gets larger.

items.prompt: A 1908 statistics paper was signed with the pen name Student. Who was behind it?

options.label: Karl Pearson, who edited the journal
Ronald Fisher, who made the distribution well known
William Gosset, an employee of a Dublin brewery
Helmert, who derived the distribution in 1876

items.explain: Gosset published under the pseudonym Student. Fisher's later work made the distribution well known under that name.

items.prompt: Brewery chemists could only afford a handful of barley measurements at a time. Why was that a fitting setting for Gosset's work?

options.label: He was interested in the problems of small samples
Barley data are always normally distributed
Large samples were banned by the brewery
Competitors demanded published proof of quality

items.explain: Gosset was interested in problems of small samples, for example the chemical properties of barley, and devised the t-test as an economical way to monitor quality.

items.prompt: A coach wants to know whether two training programs lead to different average sprint times. Which kind of test is the usual choice?

options.label: A test of whether sprint times follow a normal distribution
A t-test of whether the two group means differ
A count of how many athletes finished
A test using only one athlete's times

items.explain: The t-test's most common application is testing whether the means of two populations are significantly different.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Student's t-test checks whether the difference between how two groups respond is statistically significant. More formally, it is any hypothesis test whose test statistic follows a Student's t-distribution when the null hypothesis is true. Its most common use is to test whether the means of two populations differ significantly.

paragraphs.heading: Why not the normal curve
paragraphs.text: The test statistic would follow a normal distribution if one scaling term in it were known. Usually that term is unknown, which makes it a nuisance parameter. Once it is estimated from the data, the statistic instead has a Student's t distribution, under certain conditions. As datasets get larger the t-test converges to the Z-test, so the two often give very similar results.

paragraphs.heading: Born in a brewery
paragraphs.text: The test is named after William Sealy Gosset, who worked at the Guinness Brewery in Dublin and cared about problems with small samples, such as the chemistry of barley. He devised the t-test as a cheap way to monitor the quality of stout. In 1908 he published it in English in the journal Biometrika under the pen name Student, since his employer liked its staff to publish under pen names. Another story holds that Guinness did not want rivals to know it used the test to check raw materials. The names Student's distribution and Student's t-test became well known through the work of Ronald Fisher.

paragraphs.heading: What goes into it
paragraphs.text: A t statistic can be built from three numbers: the sample mean x̄, the sample standard deviation s and the sample size n. The test then uses n − 1 degrees of freedom. The population the data come from does not have to be normally distributed, but the distribution of sample means x̄ is assumed to be normal.

paragraphs.heading: Unpaired or paired
paragraphs.text: Two-sample t-tests come in two kinds, for independent samples or for paired ones. Suppose 100 people join a medical study and are randomly split, 50 to a treatment group and 50 to a control group; those are two independent samples, so the unpaired test fits. A paired test instead uses matched pairs of similar units, or one group measured twice. A typical case checks patients' blood pressure before and after a blood-pressure-lowering drug, so each patient serves as their own control. Strictly, the name Student's t-test belongs to the version that assumes the two populations have equal variances; without that assumption the test is sometimes called Welch's t-test.

paragraphs.heading: The price of pairing
paragraphs.text: Pairing removes the random variation between patients, so the test becomes much more likely to correctly reject a null hypothesis of no treatment effect. That gain in statistical power has a cost: every subject must be examined twice. And since each half of the sample now depends on the other, the paired version is left with just n/2 − 1 degrees of freedom, where n counts all the observations.
